explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so, friend. The psalm does start in the sanctuary: "Praise God in His sanctuary." But the very next line says, "Praise Him in His mighty heavens." (Psalm 150:1) So the call to praise doesn't stay put, and it won't stay in a bakery either.

That's right, baker! The psalm opens with "Praise God in His sanctuary," and then it keeps going. "Praise Him in His mighty heavens." (Psalm 150:1) One verse, and the praise has already walked out the front door and gone upstairs.

You got it, baker. "Praise Him for His mighty acts; praise Him for His excellent greatness." (Psalm 150:2) Each line says "for," and that little word hands you the reason. The psalm just told us where, and now it tells us why.

I see why you'd look for a time, but check the little word in the verse. "Praise Him for His mighty acts; praise Him for His excellent greatness." (Psalm 150:2) That "for" gives a reason, and there's no clock or calendar anywhere in it. I'd be the first to check a timer, friend, but this verse isn't setting one.

Nice guess, but the verse doesn't hand out a length. It says, "Praise Him for His mighty acts; praise Him for His excellent greatness." (Psalm 150:2) Both lines use "for," and that means the psalm is giving reasons. No stopwatch in this verse, friend.

Yes, baker! "Praise Him with tambourine and dancing." (Psalm 150:4) The tambourine is an instrument, but dancing is just a person moving. So the praise isn't only something you play. It's something you can do with your whole body, and I'd say that's good news for anybody who can't carry a tune.

Close, but look at the verse again, friend. "Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; praise Him with strings and flute." (Psalm 150:4) The tambourine is an instrument, and dancing is not. Dancing is just a person moving, and it's in the lineup right beside the band.

That's the one, baker! "Praise Him with clashing cymbals; praise Him with resounding cymbals." (Psalm 150:5) Cymbals that clash and resound are not tiptoeing around. I think nobody in that band was worried about waking the neighbors.

Hmm, friend, cymbals aren't known for being quiet. The verse says, "Praise Him with clashing cymbals; praise Him with resounding cymbals." (Psalm 150:5) Clashing and resounding are loud words. Nobody has ever sneaked up on somebody with a cymbal.

I can see the thought, but resounding cymbals don't stay in a closet. "Praise Him with clashing cymbals; praise Him with resounding cymbals." (Psalm 150:5) That's sound meant to carry. When something clashes and resounds, everybody nearby is going to hear it.

Yes, baker! "Let everything that has breath praise the LORD!" (Psalm 150:6) The psalm doesn't pick a job title or a section of the choir. If you've got breath in you, you're on the list, and that includes you.

Good thinking, but the psalm doesn't name priests at all. It says, "Let everything that has breath praise the LORD!" (Psalm 150:6) That's a much bigger crowd than one temple could hold. Anybody with breath gets a ticket, friend.

That's a good guess, friend, but the psalm never mentions Zion or singers here. It says, "Let everything that has breath praise the LORD!" (Psalm 150:6) Singers have breath, sure. But so does everybody else, and the call goes to all of them.

That's right, baker! The psalm opens with "Hallelujah!" and the last line ends with "Hallelujah!" (Psalm 150:1, 6) So the whole psalm is one big hallelujah with a band in the middle. It's like a cookie box with the same ribbon on both ends.

Take another look, friend. Verse 1 starts with "Hallelujah!" and verse 6 ends with "Hallelujah!" (Psalm 150:1, 6) It's the same word on both ends. Everything in between is the praise that fills the space.
